newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Crude Outlook - W.African impacts Gulf crude.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - W.African impacts Gulf crude.

text.p: A spate of West African crude cargoes recently sold into Asia could sap requirements for many June-loading Middle East crudes and keep trading light and weak in the upcoming days, traders said.
"I don't expect to see much activity for Gulf crudes taking place until a round of trading in West African crudes is completed," a trader with a Japanese oil refiner said.
The West African imports are also likely to impact appetite for regional grades, from the light sweet Tapis market to the heavier Minas market.
Many Asian traders -- most notably China and South Korea -- have been actively seeking West African crudes which have become more economically attractive with Brent's weakness.
Just last week, a South Korean refinery was believed to have purchased Angola's Palanca and Nigeria's Bonny Light cargoes to make up a very large crude carrier of crude.

Elsewhere, a Japanese refinery said it had purchased West African crudes. Although it declined to provide the name of the crude some market participants believe the company had bought a VLCC Bonny Light and Bonny Medium crude.
Japanese traders are less common buyers of West African crudes, but a few said that they had been offered cargoes and were studying the possibility of making purchases.
Traders said the purchases of West African crudes will mean less requirements for Gulf crudes in June, which was already looking weak.
"West African crudes is likely to be the key in shaping the June market for Middle East crudes," a trader with another leading Japanese oil refinery said.

He added that the purchases of West African crudes could even lead to an extra availability of Middle East crude on the spot market. Asian buyers could decide to purchase West African crude and sell their term cargoes of Gulf crudes, he said.
"My conclusion is that the market's going to look dull," the trader said.

One Western trader estimated that as much as 700,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) of West African crudes could now be heading to Asia. There are many times of the year when very little comes to Asia, he said.
Potential buyers of Gulf crudes remained relaxed last week on expectation that prices would be weak for June-loading cargoes.

Refining capacity on turnaround will fall in June, but many traders said that was unlikely to lead to an increase in requirements among end-users, many of whom appear to have relatively high stocks of oil products.

Among Middle East crudes, Oman is expected to suffer the heaviest blow in June. The crude's differential with Asia's benchmark Dubai only narrowed by a dissapointing five cents to $1.00 for June trading

The differential for many other Middle East crudes came in Bids for June Oman were mostly indicated at a discount of 10 cents to the official selling price last week, down from May trading when the crude was traded at prices ranging from MPM minus five cents to flat.
Abu Dhabi grades did not attract much discussion last week.
The market for June trading began with a handful of deals for Masila crude last week, which is mainly sold linked to dated Brent making it an attractive crude to trade with Brent's weakness.
The purchase of Masila, which competes with Oman in the market, was another factor indicating Oman's lack of popularity.
Trading in Asian crudes was mostly quiet last week with China, which often buys regional crude, seeking West African cargoes.
